builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent
summary: ExLabel replaces static, generic LLM rubrics and costly manual annotation for assessing SWE-bench-style task clarity and test coverage with an experience-bank-guided LLM assessor. Its cost is the added pipeline complexity of building, maintaining, retrieving from, and updating the experience bank, plus ongoing LLM inference or API spend for each assessed instance. It can fail if the distilled experience encodes dataset-specific biases, drifts across languages or repositories, or mislabels borderline instances, leading to filtered training data that improves benchmark results without improving production robustness.
rationale: The method is plausibly useful for constrained teams that need scalable dataset screening, but its benchmark gains should be validated on the reader's own repositories, languages, and tolerance for annotation errors before adoption.
technique: Self-evolving LLM labeler for SWE dataset quality

claims.statement: ExLabel replaces static, generic LLM rubrics and costly manual annotation for assessing SWE-bench-style task clarity and test coverage with an experience-bank-guided LLM assessor. Its cost is the added pipeline complexity of building, maintaining, retrieving from, and updating the experience bank, plus ongoing LLM inference or API spend for each assessed instance. It can fail if the distilled experience encodes dataset-specific biases, drifts across languages or repositories, or mislabels borderline instances, leading to filtered training data that improves benchmark results without improving production robustness.

Reports the best F1 across three backbone LLMs for task clarity and test coverage assessment, with relative F1 improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline on Python/Multilingual subsets; a coding model fine-tuned on ExLabel-filtered SWE-rebench data resolves 66.2% of SWE-bench Verified issues, outperforming the best baseline-filtered model by 14.5%.
